The "Summary of Attack Methods" section of the paper provides an overview of the attack methods used in the study, including the following:

1. BERT-Attack: This method uses a pre-trained BERT model to generate adversarial examples by replacing tokens in the input text with their synonyms.
2. TextFooler: This method uses a pre-trained language model to generate adversarial examples by replacing tokens in the input text with their semantically similar words.
3. SDM-Attack: This method uses a pre-trained language model to generate adversarial examples by replacing tokens in the input text with their syntactically similar words.
4. TF-Attack: This method uses an external third-party overseer, such as ChatGPT, to identify important units within sentences and generate adversarial examples by replacing entire words within the same priority queue.

section: Introduction to the Mechanism of Success

Sure, here is the summary for the Introduction to the Mechanism of Success section of the paper:

The paper analyzes the core mechanisms of previous predominant adversarial attack methodologies and identifies two substantial limitations: poor transferability and significant time overhead, particularly when applied to large language models (LLMs). The authors reveal that the distributions of importance score differ markedly among victim models, restricting the transferability, and the sequential attack processes induce substantial time overheads. Based on these insights, the authors introduce a new scheme, named TF-ATTACK, for transferable and fast adversarial attacks on LLMs. TF-ATTACK employs an external third-party overseer to identify critical units within sentences and introduces the concept of Importance Level, which allows for parallel substitutions of attacks, resulting in significant speed improvements and improved transferability.

Sure, here is the summary for the Related Work section of the paper:

The Related Work section of the paper provides an overview of previous research on adversarial attacks against large language models (LLMs). The authors highlight two main limitations of existing methods: poor transferability and slow speed. They analyze the causes of these limitations and identify distinct importance score distributions among various victim models as the primary reason for poor transferability. Additionally, they observe that over 80% of processing time is spent on sequential word-by-word operations when attacking LLMs, which slows down the attack process.

To address these limitations, the authors propose a new scheme called TF-ATTACK, which employs an external third-party overseer to identify important units within sentences and introduces the concept of Importance Level to parallelize substitutions. They also employ two tricks, Multi-Disturb and Dynamic-Disturb, to enhance attack effectiveness and transferability. The authors conduct experiments on six widely adopted benchmarks and show that TF-ATTACK surpasses previous methods in transferability and speed. Overall, the Related Work section provides a comprehensive overview of previous research on adversarial attacks against LLMs and highlights the limitations and shortcomings of existing methods, which the authors aim to address with their proposed TF-ATTACK method.
